propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review of senior immigration officer's refusal of permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds under section 25(1) of the Act.
propositions.quote: The Applicants, Peiyi Lin and her son, Zixuan (Sam) Wen, seek judicial review of the September 17, 2020 decision of a senior immigration officer [the Officer], which refused their application for permanent residence from within Canada on humanitarian and compassionate [H&C] grounds, pursuant to section 25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [the Act].

paragraphs.summary: Applicants seek judicial review of officer's refusal of permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds under section 25(1) of the Act, court states.

propositions.text: Application for Judicial Review is allowed due to flawed best interests of child assessment and unsupported findings by the Officer.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, the Application for Judicial Review is allowed. The Officer’s assessment of the best interests of Sam does not reflect the guidance of the jurisprudence and includes findings not supported by the evidence and based on speculation.

propositions.text: A flawed best interests of a child assessment cannot support the reasonableness of the overall humanitarian and compassionate decision.
propositions.quote: While the assessment of the best interests of a child [BIOC] are not necessarily determinative of whether an H&C exemption is warranted in the overall circumstances, a flawed BIOC assessment cannot support the reasonableness of the overall decision.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows judicial review because officer's best interests of child assessment is flawed and unsupported, which undermines overall decision reasonableness.

propositions.text: Applicants are Chinese citizens who arrived in Canada in 2011.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are citizens of China who arrived in Canada in 2011.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants are Chinese citizens who arrived in Canada in 2011, court states.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin had a troubled relationship with ex-husband, faced discrimination as single mother, resulting in depression and anxiety.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin recounts in her affidavit that she had a troubled relationship with her ex-husband in China. Ms. Lin states that following her divorce in 2007, she faced discrimination as a single mother, resulting in depression and anxiety.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin began practicing Falun Gong in June 2010 to improve mental health.
propositions.quote: She states that she took up the practice of Falun Gong in June 2010 in an effort to improve her mental health.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin states she faced discrimination and depression after divorce and began practicing Falun Gong in 2010 to improve mental health.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin and Sam came to Canada on August 13, 2011; refugee claim based on Falun Gong persecution was refused in May 2013.
propositions.quote: On August 13, 2011, Ms. Lin and Sam came to Canada. Their claim for refugee protection on the basis of persecution of Falun Gong practitioners was refused in May 2013.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin and Sam came to Canada in 2011; their refugee claim was refused in 2013, court states.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin reported to CBSA in Feb 2014 to sign voluntary departure but did not appear for removal after son's distress; arrest warrant issued in March 2014.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin recounts that she reported to the Canada Border Services Agency in February 2014 to sign a voluntary departure form. However, after witnessing her son’s distress at the prospect of leaving Canada, she decided not to appear for removal. A warrant was issued for her arrest in March 2014.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin reported to CBSA in 2014 but did not appear for removal due to son's distress; arrest warrant issued, court states.

propositions.text: Applicants' first H&C permanent residence application was refused in July 2017.
propositions.quote: The Applicants’ first application for permanent residence on H&C grounds was refused in July 2017.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants' first humanitarian and compassionate application was refused in 2017, court states.

propositions.text: Applicants applied again for permanent residence on H&C grounds in January 2019, relying on establishment, best interests of Sam, mental health, and adverse country conditions.
propositions.quote: The Applicants again applied for permanent residence from within Canada on H&C grounds on January 21, 2019. They relied on their establishment in Canada, the best interests of Sam, who was 16 at the time, mental health considerations, and adverse country conditions in China.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants reapplied for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds in 2019, citing establishment, best interests, mental health, and country conditions.

propositions.text: Officer found some factors favored Applicants but circumstances did not warrant exemption under section 25(1) of the Act.
propositions.quote: The Officer found that while there were some factors weighing in favour of the Applicants, their circumstances did not warrant an exemption under section 25(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found some favorable factors but denied exemption under section 25(1), court reports.

propositions.text: Officer gave some positive weight to Applicants' establishment but found it mitigated by unauthorized stay and failure to report for pre-removal interview.
propositions.quote: The Officer began by attributing “some positive weight” to the Applicants’ establishment. The Officer acknowledged that Ms. Lin and Sam had been in Canada for nine years and that Ms. Lin had been employed and self-sufficient since January 2014. The Officer noted the letters of support from Ms. Lin’s ESL teacher, the organization at which she volunteers, and an aunt, cousin, and friends in Canada. The Officer found that these relationships could be maintained from a distance. The Officer also found that the fact that the Applicants had remained in Canada without authorization and failed to report for a pre-removal interview mitigated the positive elements of their establishment. The Officer went on to note that their establishment is what would be expected of others in their circumstances. The Officer concluded that based on the evidence, “little weight” should be attributed to the establishment factor.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave some weight to establishment but mitigated by unauthorized stay and failure to report; overall little weight given, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer gave some weight to Sam's best interests, noting his high school completion, university plans, community involvement, and support letters.
propositions.quote: The Officer gave “some weight” to Sam’s best interests. The Officer noted that by the time of the decision, Sam had successfully completed high school and planned to attend university in Canada. The Officer noted Sam’s active involvement in Scouts and his participation in volunteer events and commended Sam for his achievements. The Officer acknowledged the letters of support from Sam’s friends, fellow Scouts, and friends of his mother that spoke of how Sam was a mentor to their children. The Officer found that Sam would able to remain in contact with his friends remotely.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave some weight to Sam's best interests, noting education, community involvement, and support letters, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer found Sam could reintegrate into Chinese education despite language and exam challenges, supported by family and his tutoring experience.
propositions.quote: The Officer did not agree that Sam would be unable to reintegrate into the Chinese education system due to his language level and the highly competitive university entrance examinations. The Officer found that Sam’s successful adaptation in Canada, at the age of nine, indicated that he would likely be able to adapt to life in China. The Officer also found that Sam would have the support of his mother, grandparents, and extended family. The Officer noted that Sam had tutored a friend in Chinese and concluded that his Chinese language skills were likely adequate. The Officer found that if Sam wanted to pursue post-secondary education, he would be able to update his language skills to take the entrance examinations, or he could study abroad.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Sam likely able to reintegrate into Chinese education with family support and adequate language skills, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged lack of relationship with father but found family reunification with both parents in China in Sam's best interests.
propositions.quote: The Officer acknowledged the evidence that Sam did not have a relationship with his father in China. However, the Officer found that family reunification is a significant factor and that it would be in Sam’s best interests to have access to both parents, which could occur upon return to China.

paragraphs.summary: Officer acknowledged no relationship with father but found family reunification with both parents in China in Sam's best interests, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer found little evidence corroborating Ms. Lin's Falun Gong practice and gave little weight to adverse country conditions, noting anti-discrimination laws in China.
propositions.quote: With respect to the Applicant’s submissions regarding adverse country conditions, the Officer noted that there was little evidence to corroborate Ms. Lin’s Falun Gong practice. The Officer acknowledged Ms. Lin’s submission that she would have difficulty finding work in China, including because her nursing licence had expired, and acknowledged that women may face discrimination in employment in China, but found that recourse against discrimination would be available. The Officer referred to an article that described the anti-discrimination provisions of the Chinese constitution and noted that some women had successfully sued employers for discrimination in Chinese courts.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found little evidence of Falun Gong practice and gave little weight to adverse country conditions, noting anti-discrimination laws, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer noted H&C exemptions are not intended to remedy differences in standard of living between Canada and other countries, giving little weight to adverse country conditions.
propositions.quote: In concluding that the adverse country conditions warranted “little weight,” the Officer noted that H&C exemptions are not intended to remedy differences in the standard of living between Canada and other countries.

paragraphs.summary: Officer noted H&C exemptions do not address standard of living differences, giving little weight to adverse country conditions, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged mental health issues but found little evidence of prior treatment or unavailability of treatment in China.
propositions.quote: The Officer also gave other relevant factors “little weight.” With respect to the Applicants’ submissions about their mental health, the Officer acknowledged the psychotherapist’s opinion that the Applicants suffer from anxiety and depressive symptoms due to their fear of being forced to leave Canada. The Officer also noted Ms. Lin’s account of her psychological state throughout and since her marriage. The Officer found that there was little evidence showing the Applicants had sought assistance for their mental health either in China or in Canada prior to their meeting with the psychotherapist for the purpose of their H&C application. The Officer also found that there was no evidence that treatment would be unavailable in China or that Ms. Lin would not be able to access such treatment discreetly.

paragraphs.summary: Officer acknowledged mental health issues but found little evidence of prior treatment or unavailability of treatment in China, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicants resourceful and likely able to reintegrate into Chinese society and labour market, with possible short-term family support and savings.
propositions.quote: The Officer acknowledged that relocation to China might be challenging, but concluded that the Applicants are resourceful and well-educated individuals who could transfer their knowledge and skills obtained in Canada to the Chinese labour market and would likely be able to reintegrate and re-establish themselves in Chinese society. The Officer also acknowledged the letters from family members in China stating that the family could not financially assist the Applicants, but concluded that there was no evidence that their family members would not provide short-term support. The Officer noted that the Applicants could rely on their savings.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicants resourceful and likely able to reintegrate in China with possible family support and savings, court reports.

propositions.text: Applicants argue decision is unreasonable due to flawed BIOC assessment, ignoring relevant evidence, and overly stringent H&C test.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit that the decision is not reasonable because the Officer erred in the assessment of the BIOC, ignored relevant evidence, and more generally applied an overly stringent test in determining whether the H&C exemption was warranted which does not reflect the compassionate and empathetic approach guiding H&C determinations.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue decision is unreasonable due to flawed best interests of child assessment, ignored evidence, and overly stringent H&C test.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Officer failed to consider psychological and emotional trauma to Sam from removal and loss of in-person contact.
propositions.quote: With respect to the Officer’s assessment of Sam’s best interests, the Applicants argue that the Officer failed to meaningfully consider the psychological and emotional trauma that removal would impose on him given, among other things, his integration into his community and school, and his loss of access to education in China.

propositions.text: Applicants argue remote relationships are not substitutes for in-person contact, especially for family and young persons.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue that maintaining relationships from a distance is not a substitute for in-person contact, particularly for family and young persons.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Officer turned Sam’s attributes against him by finding he could easily readapt in China.
propositions.quote: The Applicants further submit that the Officer turned Sam’s attributes and resourcefulness against him in finding that he could easily readapt in China.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer failed to consider trauma from removal, remote contact is inadequate, and turned Sam's attributes against him.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Officer ignored evidence contradicting findings, e.g. Sam's inability to pursue high school in China due to missed exams and curriculum.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue the Officer ignored evidence and made findings that contradict the evidence provided. For example, they challenge the Officer’s finding that Sam would be able to overcome his lack of proficiency in Mandarin and enroll in university in China. The Applicants point to a letter from the local middle school where they formerly lived, which explains that Sam would not be able to pursue his high school education in China due to missed examinations and elements of the curriculum.

propositions.text: Applicants point to evidence of difficulty of college entry exams and extreme pressure of Chinese educational system.
propositions.quote: The Applicants also point to the evidence of the difficulty of the college entry exams and the extreme pressure of the educational system generally.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer ignored evidence contradicting findings on Sam's education and noted difficulty of Chinese exams and pressure.

propositions.text: It was perverse for the Officer to find it in Sam's best interests to be reunited with his abusive father.
propositions.quote: it was perverse for the Officer to find it would be in Sam’s best interests to be reunited with his father, given that both Ms. Lin and Sam stated that he was abusive.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants argue it was perverse for the Officer to find it in Sam's best interests to reunite with his abusive father.

propositions.text: The Officer erred by comparing their establishment to others in similar circumstances.
propositions.quote: the Officer erred in comparing their establishment to that of others in their circumstances.

propositions.text: The Officer placed undue emphasis on Ms. Lin's failure to report for removal and ignored her explanation supported by a psychotherapist's opinion.
propositions.quote: the Officer placed undue emphasis on Ms. Lin’s failure to report for removal and did not consider her explanation, which is supported by the psychotherapist’s opinion regarding Ms. Lin’s mental and emotional state at the time.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants argue the Officer erred by comparing their establishment to others and unduly emphasized Ms. Lin's failure to report removal without considering her explanation.

propositions.text: The Officer failed to distinguish Sam's circumstances as he remained in Canada without authorization for reasons beyond his control.
propositions.quote: the Officer failed to distinguish Sam’s circumstances given that he remained in Canada without authorization for reasons beyond his control.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants argue the Officer failed to distinguish Sam's unauthorized stay due to reasons beyond his control.

propositions.text: The Officer considered the Applicants' individual circumstances; the Applicants merely ask the Court to reweigh evidence.
propositions.quote: the Officer clearly considered the Applicants’ individual circumstances and that the Applicants are simply asking the Court to reweigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent submits the Officer considered the Applicants' circumstances and the Applicants ask the Court to reweigh evidence.

propositions.text: Officers are not required to cite each piece of evidence; failure to mention critical contradictory evidence may but does not necessarily imply non-consideration.
propositions.quote: officers are not required to cite each piece of evidence when rendering a decision, and that failure to mention critical evidence that contradicts the officer’s conclusion may, but does not necessarily, lead to an inference that the officer did not consider and assess the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues officers need not cite all evidence and omission of contradictory evidence does not necessarily mean it was not considered.

propositions.text: The Officer reasonably considered Sam's best interests and gave it positive weight; a positive BIOC does not determine the H&C exemption.
propositions.quote: the Officer reasonably considered Sam’s best interests and gave this factor positive weight, but that a positive BIOC does not determine the H&C exemption.

propositions.text: The Officer was not required to mention the letter from the local middle school in China as Sam had graduated high school by decision time.
propositions.quote: the Officer was not required to mention the letter from the local middle school in China because, by the time of the decision, Sam had already graduated from high school.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Officer reasonably considered Sam's best interests and was not required to mention the school letter as Sam had graduated.

propositions.text: The Officer should have addressed evidence of Sam's father's violence and neglect but this is not a fatal flaw as Sam is not obliged to reconnect with his father in China.
propositions.quote: the Respondent concedes that the Officer should have addressed the evidence of Sam’s father’s violence and neglect, but submits that this is not a fatal flaw, as nothing obliges Sam to reconnect with his father if he returns to China.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent concedes the Officer should have addressed father's violence but says it is not fatal as Sam need not reconnect with him.

propositions.text: The Officer did not err in assessing establishment against typical establishment of others with similar time in Canada.
propositions.quote: the Officer did not err in assessing the Applicants’ establishment against the level of establishment that is typical of others who have spent a similar amount of time in Canada.

propositions.text: Officers may consider residence and employment without valid immigration status; the Officer did not dismiss application solely on this basis.
propositions.quote: officers are entitled to consider an applicant’s residence and employment in Canada without valid immigration status. The Respondent adds that the Officer did not dismiss the application solely on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Officer properly assessed establishment and may consider residence without status; application was not dismissed solely for this.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy is distinguishable as Applicants lack diagnosed mental illness or greater hardship than typical removal hardship.
propositions.quote: Kanthasamy v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 [Kanthasamy], is distinguishable because the Applicants have not been diagnosed with a particular mental illness and have not shown that they will experience greater hardship than what can be reasonably expected of anyone facing removal from Canada.

propositions.text: It is not necessarily an error to consider availability of treatment in country of origin.
propositions.quote: it is not necessarily an error to consider the availability of treatment in the country of origin.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues Kanthasamy is distinguishable and it is not necessarily error to consider treatment availability in country of origin.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the Officer's decision is reasonable, including assessment of BIOC and evidence consideration in H&C exemption.
propositions.quote: The issue is whether the Officer’s decision is reasonable. This entails consideration of whether the Officer’s assessment of the BIOC reflects the guidance of the jurisprudence and whether the Officer ignored evidence and reached conclusions not supported by the evidence in assessing the relevant factors and in the overall assessment of whether the H&C exemption was warranted.

paragraphs.summary: The issue is whether the Officer's decision is reasonable, including BIOC assessment and evidence consideration for H&C exemption.

propositions.text: H&C decisions are discretionary and reviewed on reasonableness standard (Baker; Kanthasamy).
propositions.quote: H&C decisions are discretionary decisions and are reviewed on the reasonableness standard (Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817 at paras 57–62, 174 DLR (4th) 193 [Baker]; Kanthasamy at para 44).

paragraphs.summary: H&C decisions are discretionary and reviewed on reasonableness standard, per Baker and Kanthasamy.

propositions.text: Vavilov confirms reasonableness is standard for discretionary decisions and provides review guidance.
propositions.quote: In Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 16, 23 [Vavilov], the Supreme Court of Canada confirmed that reasonableness is the applicable standard of review for discretionary decisions. The Supreme Court provided extensive guidance to the courts in reviewing a decision for reasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: Vavilov confirms reasonableness is the standard for discretionary decisions and provides review guidance.

propositions.text: A reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, and justified by facts and law; perfection is not required (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision‑maker (Vavilov at paras 85, 102, 105–07). The court does not assess the reasons against a standard of perfection (Vavilov at para 91).

paragraphs.summary: A reasonable decision is coherent, rational, justified by facts and law; perfection is not required, per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Decisions should not be set aside unless serious shortcomings make them unjustified, unintelligible or non-transparent (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: In Vavilov, at para 100, the Supreme Court of Canada noted that decisions should not be set aside unless there are “sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” and that “[t]he court must be satisfied that any shortcomings or flaws relied on by the party challenging the decision are sufficiently central or significant to render the decision unreasonable.”

paragraphs.summary: Decisions should not be set aside unless serious shortcomings render them unreasonable, per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Section 25 of the Act allows discretionary H&C exemptions from inadmissibility and other criteria to avoid return to China.
propositions.quote: Section 25 of the Act provides that an exemption from some findings of inadmissibility and from other criteria or obligations of the Act may be granted on the basis of H&C considerations. This is a discretionary relief that exempts an applicant from the otherwise applicable legal requirements. In the present case, the exemption, if granted, would overcome the need to return to China and seek to immigrate to Canada in accordance with the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Section 25 allows discretionary H&C exemptions to avoid return to China and legal requirements.

propositions.text: Applicant bears onus to establish with sufficient evidence that H&C exemption should be granted.
propositions.quote: An applicant bears the onus to establish with sufficient evidence that the exemption should be granted.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant bears onus to prove H&C exemption with sufficient evidence.

propositions.text: H&C exemption is based on global assessment including best interests of affected child; varies by facts (Kanthasamy).
propositions.quote: The determination of whether an H&C exemption is justified is based on a global assessment of the relevant factors, including the best interests of any child affected by the decision. In Kanthasamy, the Supreme Court of Canada explained that what warrants relief under section 25 varies depending on the facts and context of each case.

paragraphs.summary: H&C exemption is a global assessment including child's best interests and varies by case facts, per Kanthasamy.

propositions.text: Officer may find positive factors yet deny exemption; weight of factors is discretionary; court does not reweigh but reviews for overlooked or misconstrued evidence.
propositions.quote: An officer assessing an H&C application could find several positive factors yet still conclude that the exemption is not warranted. There is no rigid formula or score assigned to each factor. The weight given to each factor or consideration is within the Officer’s discretion and it is not the role of the Court to reweigh the individual factors or the overall assessment. However, an H&C determination is not immune from review where on the particular facts, for example, the officer overlooks or misconstrues relevant evidence or makes findings that are not supported by the evidence and which would have an impact on the weight to be attributed to the relevant factors.

paragraphs.summary: Officer may deny exemption despite positive factors; weight is discretionary; court reviews for overlooked or unsupported evidence.

propositions.text: Officer must adopt compassionate approach but negative result does not imply lack of compassion; H&C relief is exceptional and discretionary.
propositions.quote: With respect to the more general argument of the Applicants that the Officer failed to adopt a compassionate approach, as required by Kanthasamy, there is nothing in the Officer’s reasons to suggest this. While a negative result could be subjectively perceived as a lack of compassion, an H&C exemption remains exceptional relief. Officers must consider all the relevant factors and weigh the positive against the negative to reach a global assessment of whether this relief is justified in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Officer must be compassionate but negative result does not mean lack of compassion; H&C relief is exceptional and discretionary.

propositions.text: Hardship from removal is normal and alone does not justify H&C exemption; more than sympathy is required (Shackleford; Huang).
propositions.quote: The jurisprudence post-Kanthasamy is consistent in finding that some hardship is the normal consequence of removal and, on its own, does not support the exemption, and that more than a sympathetic case is required to justify the exemption (see for example Shackleford v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1313 at paras 11–12, 16 [Shackleford]; Huang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 265 at paras 17–19 [Huang]).

paragraphs.summary: Hardship from removal is normal and alone insufficient for H&C exemption; more than sympathy is needed, per Shackleford and Huang.

propositions.text: Applicants for exceptional H&C relief must show misfortunes or considerations greater than typical applicants for permanent residence.
propositions.quote: an applicant for the exceptional H&C relief provided by the [Act] must demonstrate the existence or likely existence of misfortunes or other H&C considerations that are greater than those typically faced by others who apply for permanent residence in Canada

paragraphs.summary: The Chief Justice in Huang stated applicants must show misfortunes or considerations greater than typical applicants for permanent residence (prior_court_or_authority).

propositions.text: I applied jurisprudence principles governing H&C applications to assess the Officer's decision's reasonableness.
propositions.quote: I have applied the principles from the jurisprudence governing H&C applications in determining whether the Officer’s decision is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: I applied jurisprudence principles governing H&C applications to assess the Officer's decision's reasonableness (court).

propositions.text: The Officer gave varying weights to factors, making assessment of reasonableness challenging.
propositions.quote: the Officer gave “some weight” to the BIOC, “little weight” to establishment, “little weight” to adverse country conditions and “little weight” to other hardship considerations

propositions.text: Assigning weight to factors is not unusual and lacks mathematical calculation.
propositions.quote: This approach to identifying the weight attributed to the relevant factors is not unusual as there is no mathematical calculation

paragraphs.summary: The Officer gave varying weights to factors without mathematical calculation, making reasonableness assessment challenging (court).

propositions.text: The Officer made reasonable findings supported by evidence and jurisprudence.
propositions.quote: The Officer made several findings that are reasonable and are supported by the evidence and the jurisprudence.

propositions.text: The Officer also made findings unsupported by evidence, speculative, and overlooked relevant evidence.
propositions.quote: the Officer made other findings that are not supported by the evidence, that are based on speculation and that overlook relevant evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer made both reasonable findings supported by evidence and unreasonable speculative findings overlooking evidence (court).

propositions.text: The Officer reasonably considered Applicants' establishment relative to others in similar circumstances.
propositions.quote: The Officer did not err in considering the Applicants’ establishment in the context of the level of establishment that might be expected of others in similar circumstances

propositions.text: Applicants argue H&C officers should explain what constitutes exceptional establishment.
propositions.quote: the Applicants submit, more generally, that H&C officers should provide an explanation of what constitutes exceptional establishment

propositions.text: Requiring explanation of exceptional establishment would impose undue rigidity in discretionary decisions.
propositions.quote: this would impose undue rigidity in a discretionary decision where individual circumstances may vary greatly

propositions.text: Applicants argue greater consideration should be given to Sam’s establishment due to formative years in Canada.
propositions.quote: Applicants also argue that greater consideration should have been given to Sam’s establishment in Canada, as he has spent his formative years in Canada

propositions.text: Respondent says Sam’s establishment was considered in the Officer’s BIOC analysis.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that Sam’s establishment was considered in the context of the Officer’s BIOC analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer reasonably considered establishment; Applicants want explanation and more weight for Sam; Respondent says Sam’s establishment was considered (earlier_decision_maker, applicant, respondent, court).

propositions.text: The Officer reasonably considered Applicants’ unauthorized stay, missed interview, and unauthorized work.
propositions.quote: the Officer did not err in considering that the Applicants had remained in Canada without status since the refusal of their refugee claim... failed to appear for the pre-removal interview, and worked without authorization

propositions.text: Prior cases support considering unauthorized stay and work in H&C decisions.
propositions.quote: Legault v Canada... Joseph v Canada... Choi v Canada... Shackleford at paras 23–25

propositions.text: The Officer did not treat this factor as determinative but considered it with other establishment aspects.
propositions.quote: The Officer did not focus on this factor as determinative, but rather considered this along with the other aspects of the Applicants’ establishment.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer reasonably considered unauthorized stay and work, supported by prior cases, but not as determinative (earlier_decision_maker, prior_court_or_authority).

propositions.text: The Officer reasonably assessed the psychotherapist’s report on Applicants’ mental health, especially Ms. Lin’s.
propositions.quote: the Officer’s assessment is reasonable. A report or opinion on an applicant’s mental health for the purpose of an H&C exemption should be closely scrutinized and the Officer did so

propositions.text: Mental health reports for H&C exemptions require close scrutiny.
propositions.quote: A report or opinion on an applicant’s mental health for the purpose of an H&C exemption should be closely scrutinized

paragraphs.summary: The Officer reasonably assessed the psychotherapist’s report on mental health, applying required close scrutiny (earlier_decision_maker, prior_court_or_authority).

propositions.text: Ms. Lin described psychological distress in China, impact on relationship, and improvements in Canada.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin had described the psychological distress she experienced in China, its impact on her relationship with Sam, and the improvements since they have been in Canada.

propositions.text: Psychotherapist noted Ms. Lin’s severe anxiety, moderate depression, and suicidal ideation.
propositions.quote: The psychotherapist’s report noted that Ms. Lin continues to suffer from severe anxiety and moderate depressive symptoms, and expressed concern about Ms. Lin’s reported suicidal ideation.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin described psychological distress and improvements; psychotherapist reported severe anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation (witness_or_document).

propositions.text: The Officer accepted Ms. Lin’s mental health findings but found no persuasive evidence she couldn’t access discreet treatment in China.
propositions.quote: The Officer reasonably found that there was no persuasive evidence that Ms. Lin could not access mental health services discreetly, if needed, in China.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer accepted Ms. Lin’s mental health issues but found no evidence she couldn’t access discreet treatment in China (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: The Officer made speculative findings about family support, employment prospects, and legal recourse in China unsupported by evidence.
propositions.quote: the Officer made other findings that are based on speculation and that do not reflect the evidence before the Officer, including that the Applicants’ family in China could provide short-term support, that Ms. Lin could find employment, and that she had recourse through the courts if she faced discrimination in employment.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer made speculative, unsupported findings about family support, employment, and legal recourse in China (court).

propositions.text: Applicants bear the onus to establish H&C exemption but cannot anticipate all Officer conclusions to rebut.
propositions.quote: There is no dispute that the onus is on the Applicants to establish that the H&C exemption is warranted. However, it is a challenge for any applicant to anticipate the conclusions an Officer may reach and to proffer evidence to rebut conclusions that are not based on evidence.

propositions.text: Applicants did not provide evidence on feasibility of Sam studying abroad as they could not anticipate Officer’s finding.
propositions.quote: the Applicants did not provide evidence regarding whether it would be feasible for Sam to study abroad as they could not likely have anticipated that the Officer would so find

propositions.text: Ms. Lin asserted she could not find employment and family could not provide financial support.
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin asserted that she would be unable to find employment in China and that her family could not provide any financial support.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants bear onus but cannot anticipate all Officer conclusions; they lacked evidence on Sam studying abroad; Ms. Lin said no employment or family support (court, applicant).

propositions.text: The Officer’s BIOC analysis is a serious shortcoming making the decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the serious shortcoming in the Officer’s decision, which leads the Court to find that in the particular circumstances the decision is not reasonable, is the BIOC analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer’s BIOC analysis is a serious shortcoming rendering the decision unreasonable (court).

propositions.text: BIOC is important in H&C applications affecting children; Sam was a child at 16 and his best interests matter.
propositions.quote: BIOC is an important factor in an H&C application where children are directly affected—and although Sam was 16 at the time of the application, he was nonetheless a child and his best interests are important.

propositions.text: Baker principles on children’s best interests continue to apply in H&C decisions.
propositions.quote: The principles established in Baker continue to apply (Kanthasamy at paras 38–39).

paragraphs.summary: BIOC is important for children in H&C; Sam was a child; Baker principles apply (court, prior_court_or_authority).

propositions.text: Decision-makers must consider children’s best interests substantially; minimizing them is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Decision-makers must “consider children’s best interests as an important factor, give them substantial weight, and be alert, alive and sensitive to them” (Baker at para 75). A child’s best interests need not be determinative nor necessarily outweigh other considerations, but a decision that inappropriately minimizes the child’s interests will be unreasonable (Baker).

paragraphs.summary: Decision-makers must substantially consider children’s best interests; minimizing them is unreasonable (prior_court_or_authority).

propositions.text: Respondent agrees BIOC assessment approach in Williams is not rigid or formulaic.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that the approach to assessing BIOC, noted in Williams... is not a rigid or required formula.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent agrees BIOC assessment approach in Williams is not rigid or formulaic (respondent).

propositions.text: Justice Pentney noted no single formula should be required for discretionary BIOC decisions.
propositions.quote: it would be contrary to the teachings of the Supreme Court in Baker and Kanthasamy... to require an Officer to follow one particular formula for such an inherently discretionary decision.

paragraphs.summary: Justice Pentney noted no single formula should be required for discretionary BIOC decisions (prior_court_or_authority).

propositions.text: BIOC assessment should be contextual, responsive to child’s age, capacity, needs, and maturity.
propositions.quote: The assessment of the best interests of a child should be highly contextual and responsive to each child’s particular age, capacity, needs, and maturity

paragraphs.summary: BIOC assessment should be contextual and responsive to child’s age, capacity, needs, and maturity (prior_court_or_authority).

propositions.text: BIOC must be well identified, defined, and examined with great attention in light of all evidence.
propositions.quote: Those interests must be “well identified and defined” and examined “with a great deal of attention” in light of all the evidence

paragraphs.summary: BIOC must be well identified, defined, and examined with great attention considering all evidence (prior_court_or_authority).

propositions.text: Officer noted Sam’s achievements but did not clearly identify or define Sam’s best interests.
propositions.quote: the Officer addressed various aspects of Sam’s achievements... However, the Officer did not clearly identify or define what was in Sam’s best interests.

propositions.text: Attributing “some weight” to BIOC does not clearly show Officer found Sam’s best interests to remain in Canada.
propositions.quote: The attribution of “some weight” to BIOC does not even clearly convey that the Officer found that Sam’s best interests were to remain in Canada.

propositions.text: Officer’s reasons for “some weight” do not explain how that finding was reached.
propositions.quote: the Officer’s reasons for finding “some weight” do not convey how that finding was arrived at.

propositions.text: No rigid formula exists to assess BIOC but reasons must convey basis for findings.
propositions.quote: Although I accept that there is no rigid formula to assess BIOC, the Officer’s reasons for finding “some weight” do not convey how that finding was arrived at.

paragraphs.summary: Officer noted Sam’s achievements but failed to clearly identify or explain Sam’s best interests or basis for BIOC weight (earlier_decision_maker, court).

propositions.text: Officer made erroneous findings on Sam’s education and reunification benefits and overlooked psychological impact of removal.
propositions.quote: the Officer made erroneous findings in the BIOC assessment regarding Sam’s ability to upgrade his education in China or study abroad and regarding the benefits of reunification with his father. The Officer also overlooked the psychological impact on Sam of his potential removal as described by the psychotherapist.

propositions.text: These BIOC analysis shortcomings lead to the overall decision being unreasonable.
propositions.quote: I consider these findings to be serious shortcomings in the BIOC analysis, which leads to the conclusion that the overall decision is not reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Officer made erroneous BIOC findings and overlooked psychological impact, making the overall decision unreasonable (court).

propositions.text: Sam was doing well academically in Canada and had applied to Canadian universities
propositions.quote: The evidence before the Officer demonstrated that Sam was doing well academically in Canada and had applied to Canadian universities

propositions.text: If returned to China, Sam would not be eligible to apply to attend universities there
propositions.quote: but if returned to China, he would not be eligible to apply to attend universities there

propositions.text: Officer's finding that Sam could upgrade Chinese skills and gain entrance to Chinese university is contradicted by evidence
propositions.quote: Contrary to the Officer’s finding, it is not simply a matter of upgrading his Chinese language skills. The Officer’s finding that Sam could do so and gain entrance to a Chinese university is contradicted by the evidence

propositions.text: Officer's finding that Sam could seek to study abroad is speculative and unsupported by evidence
propositions.quote: The Officer’s finding that he could, alternatively, seek to study abroad is speculative and is not supported by any evidence

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found Sam academically successful in Canada but ineligible for Chinese universities; court finds these findings contradicted or speculative.

propositions.text: Ms. Lin stated Sam could not speak Mandarin fluently and never learned to write Chinese properly
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin stated that Sam could not speak Mandarin fluently and that he had never learned to write Chinese properly

propositions.text: Officer did not refer to local middle school letter or objective evidence about difficulty of Chinese university entrance exams
propositions.quote: The Officer did not refer either to the letter from the local middle school nor to the objective evidence that the university entrance exams are extremely difficult

propositions.text: Respondent argues Officer not required to consider school letter since Sam graduated high school
propositions.quote: The Respondent points out that Sam had already graduated high school and argues that the Officer was therefore not required to consider the letter from the school

propositions.text: Objective evidence and letter suggest Sam would have to begin high school anew in China to gain university entrance
propositions.quote: the objective evidence, including the letter, suggests that this would not be sufficient to gain entrance to university in China and that Sam would have to begin high school anew

propositions.text: No evidence it would be feasible financially or otherwise for Sam to study abroad
propositions.quote: there was no evidence that it would be feasible, financially or otherwise, for Sam to seek to study abroad

propositions.text: Applicants could not anticipate need to rebut Officer's speculative conclusion about studying abroad
propositions.quote: the Applicants could not anticipate the need to rebut this type of conclusion

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Lin said Sam lacks Mandarin fluency; Officer ignored school letter and evidence; Respondent says letter not needed; court finds Sam must restart high school in China and no evidence supports studying abroad.

propositions.text: Officer found it in Sam's best interests to have access to both parents, contrary to evidence
propositions.quote: The Officer also found, contrary to the evidence, that it would be in Sam’s best interests to “have access to both parents.”

propositions.text: Ms. Lin's affidavit said Sam's father had little involvement; Sam opposed relationship with father
propositions.quote: Ms. Lin’s affidavit attested that Sam’s father had little to do with him and Sam’s own letter vehemently opposed any relationship with his father

propositions.text: Officer's generic finding of family reunification benefit based only on Officer's opinion
propositions.quote: The Officer’s generic finding of “family reunification to be a significant factor” is based only on the Officer’s opinion about what is best for this family

paragraphs.summary: Officer found family reunification best for Sam despite evidence Sam opposes father; court finds Officer's view was opinion only.

propositions.text: Respondent notes Sam's age means he can choose contact with father
propositions.quote: As the Respondent notes, given Sam’s age, he would have a choice whether to pursue contact with his father

propositions.text: Officer's opinion on family reunification influenced overall assessment and is invalid here
propositions.quote: the Officer’s opinion about the benefits of family reunification had a bearing on the overall assessment and is not a valid consideration in this particular case

paragraphs.summary: Respondent says Sam can choose contact with father; court finds Officer's family reunification opinion invalid and influential.

propositions.text: Best interests of child assessment must consider child's views per age and maturity (Hawthorne, Huang)
propositions.quote: An assessment of the best interests of a child should be sensitive to the views of the child, in accordance with their age and maturity: Hawthorne v Canada... Huang at para 25

propositions.text: Mature minor's views get significant weight; officer should not substitute own views (Huang)
propositions.quote: Although a “mature minor person’s” views are not determinative, significant weight should be given to their expression of their interests, and an officer should not substitute their own views (Huang at para 31)

propositions.text: Sam clearly expressed views about return to China and father, which were not given due consideration
propositions.quote: Sam had clearly set out his views about the impact of returning to China in his letter, including his views about his father, which appear not to have been given due consideration

paragraphs.summary: Law requires considering child's views; Sam expressed views not properly considered by Officer.

propositions.text: Officer not required to address every evidence piece, especially in voluminous application
propositions.quote: I acknowledge that the Officer was not required to address every piece of evidence, particularly, as noted by the Respondent, in a very voluminous application

propositions.text: Psychotherapist's report was highlighted and addressed re Ms. Lin but not re Sam's best interests
propositions.quote: the report of the psychotherapist was highlighted in the H&C submissions and the Officer addressed the report, but with a focus on Ms. Lin. The Officer did not address the psychotherapist’s opinion with respect to Sam in the context of the assessment of his best interests

paragraphs.summary: Officer need not address all evidence; psychotherapist's report addressed for Ms. Lin but not for Sam's best interests.

propositions.text: Psychotherapist reported Sam has moderate anxiety and depression; Ms. Lin's anxiety impacts Sam
propositions.quote: The psychotherapist’s report noted that Sam exhibits moderate symptoms of anxiety and depression and that Ms. Lin’s anxiety also has an impact on Sam

propositions.text: Psychotherapist said uprooting Sam will significantly and negatively impact him moving from stable to insecure situation
propositions.quote: The psychotherapist explained that “uprooting” Sam will significantly and negatively impact him as he moves from a stable to an insecure situation

propositions.text: Law requires Officer to consider if psychotherapist's opinion is inherent consequence of removal or beyond; Officer did not do so
propositions.quote: it was incumbent on the Officer to consider whether the psychotherapist’s opinion fell within the inherent consequences of removal or went beyond. The Officer appears not to have done so

paragraphs.summary: Psychotherapist reported Sam's anxiety and negative impact of uprooting; Officer failed to consider if this exceeded inherent removal consequences.

propositions.text: Strong positive best interests assessment not determinative of H&C application
propositions.quote: I acknowledge that even a strong positive assessment of the best interests of a child is not necessarily determinative of an H&C application

propositions.text: Officer attributed 'some weight' to best interests but did not clarify how much or clearly identify Sam's best interests
propositions.quote: attributing “some weight”—even in contrast to “little weight” attributed to other factors—does not indicate how much weight the Officer attached to the BIOC

propositions.text: Errors in Officer's best interests analysis mean greater weight might have impacted overall H&C assessment
propositions.quote: Given that the Officer’s analysis of the BIOC does not clearly identify Sam’s best interests and coupled with the errors in the Officer’s BIOC analysis, if properly assessed, the BIOC may have warranted greater weight, and that greater weight could have had an impact on the overall assessment of whether the H&C exemption was justified

paragraphs.summary: Best interests assessment not determinative; Officer gave unclear weight; errors mean greater weight might affect H&C outcome.

propositions.text: H&C application must be redetermined by a different officer
propositions.quote: As a result, the H&C application must be redetermined by a different officer

propositions.text: Judicial review application is allowed
propositions.quote: The Application for Judicial Review is allowed

propositions.text: No question proposed for certification and none arises
propositions.quote: No question was proposed for certification and none arises

paragraphs.summary: Court allows judicial review, orders H&C application redetermined by different officer, no certification question arises.
